title: Wall painting from Room F of the Villa of P. Fannius Synistor at Boscoreale

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1903

altText: A Roman wall painting in fresco showing painted architecture with columns, made to make a flat wall look like a deeper, built space.

context: A fresco from a room in a villa at Boscoreale, near Pompeii in southern Italy, painted around 50-40 BCE. Boscoreale was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE, which preserved the paintings, and the Met acquired this set in 1903.

descriptions.k: This is a wall painting from a house in ancient Rome. It shows tall columns. The artist painted them on a flat wall. Can you see how they look like real ones? Where would you stand to look at them?
descriptions.g12: This painting was made on a wall in a Roman villa about 2,000 years ago. The artist painted columns, so a flat wall looks like a real building with space behind it. Fresco means paint put on wet plaster. A volcano later buried the villa, and that kept the wall safe. How does the artist trick your eyes?
descriptions.g35: A Roman painter made this fresco, painted on wet plaster, for a room in a villa at Boscoreale near Pompeii. It shows columns, and the painter used shading and lines to make the flat wall look like it has depth. A volcano, Mount Vesuvius, buried the villa in 79 CE and protected the paintings. Look at how the columns seem to stand forward. What makes them look three-dimensional?
descriptions.g68: Painted around 50-40 BCE, this fresco from the Villa of P. Fannius Synistor belongs to a style of Roman wall painting that imitates architecture, so that a plain room seems to open into grand spaces. The painter uses perspective and shading to turn the flat wall into columns and ledges. Vesuvius's eruption in 79 CE buried the villa and preserved the paintings, but we do not know all about the painter. Why would someone want painted architecture in their own home?
descriptions.g910: This fresco is an example of illusionistic wall painting in a Roman villa: instead of decorating a surface, the painter appears to dissolve it by showing architecture where none exists. Columns, shading, and perspective create a theatrical effect, suggesting wealth and sophistication. The wall survived because the eruption of Vesuvius buried the villa. Consider how a viewer moving through the room would experience the painted space. How does this illusion reflect the Roman desire to display culture and status at home?
descriptions.g1112: The wall paintings from Boscoreale preserve a decorative system in which flat surfaces are made to read as architecture, a program often discussed in relation to Roman ideas of luxury, theater, and domestic display. The excavation context, and the later removal of the paintings to museums, complicates how they are seen today, since the room as a lived whole has been taken apart. Which parts of the original experience can we reconstruct, and which are lost? The fresco invites reflection on illusion, status, and the ethics of collecting ancient art.

g1112.shape: How do repeating architectural shapes create rhythm that works across the whole room?
g1112.color: How do color and tone represent materials, and how might ancient pigments and aging have altered the effect?
g1112.texture: How does the fresco's imitation of material surfaces relate to broader Roman interest in illusion?
g1112.space: How does the blurring of real and painted space reflect ideas about theater, display, and domestic life?
g1112.light: How does the painted treatment of light create a fictional light source, and what does this suggest about pictorial priorities?
g1112.meaning: How do Roman wall painting styles register social aspiration, and what are the risks of reading them as direct evidence of wealth?
g1112.culture: How do the circumstances of Vesuvius's eruption complicate our sense of Roman art as representative of the wider empire?
g1112.technique: What do the technical demands of fresco imply about workshops, planning, and collaboration?

g1112.critical: How should scholars treat fragments and reconstructed contexts when drawing conclusions about ancient interiors?

teacherNote.context: A Roman fresco of about 50-40 BCE from Room F of a villa at Boscoreale near Pompeii, acquired by the Met in 1903. Frescoes are painted onto wet plaster, and the villa was buried by Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE.
directions: Have students draw a flat wall, then add columns with shading to make it look deep.
Discuss how a volcano can preserve a place and what we learn from preserved homes.
Compare painted illusion with a modern digital backdrop or a mural that tricks the eye.
